summary: The dreaded reunion becomes a reconciliation. Seeing Esau approach with his four hundred men, Jacob arranges his family in order of protection and "bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother." But Esau, so long feared, "ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." When Esau asks about the family, Jacob answers that they are "the children which God hath graciously given thy servant." Esau at first refuses the lavish gift, saying "I have enough, my brother," but Jacob presses him: "receive my present at my hand: for therefore I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God, and thou wast pleased with me." Esau relents and takes it. Jacob gently declines to travel together, promising to follow "softly" for the sake of the tender children and young flocks, and Esau returns to Seir. Rather than following to Seir, Jacob journeys to Succoth and builds booths, then comes to Shechem in Canaan, buys a parcel of land, and erects an altar he calls El-elohe-Israel, "God, the God of Israel."
takeaways: The feared brother becomes an instrument of grace; Esau's embrace shows God can soften hearts that seemed set on vengeance.
Jacob sees the face of God reflected in his reconciled brother, linking human forgiveness to divine mercy.
Jacob credits his family entirely to God's graciousness, echoing his transformation at Peniel.
Building an altar named El-elohe-Israel marks Jacob's return to the land as a worshipper claiming God as his own.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 32:28-30 — Israel sees God face to face at Peniel
crossRefs.why: Jacob tells Esau he has seen his face "as though I had seen the face of God," deliberately echoing his encounter at Peniel the night before. The reconciled human face becomes a sign of the divine favor he just received.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 27:41-45 — Esau's earlier resolve to kill Jacob
crossRefs.why: Esau had once vowed to slay Jacob for stealing his blessing, driving Jacob into exile. The tearful embrace here shows the full reversal of that hatred and closes the long arc of the brothers' conflict.

crossRefs.label: Luke 15:20 — the father runs and falls on the son's neck
crossRefs.why: The prodigal's father "ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him," language that closely mirrors Esau running to embrace Jacob. Christian readers hear an anticipation of the gospel picture of joyful reconciliation.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 34:1-2 — Dinah goes out at Shechem
crossRefs.why: Jacob's settling near Shechem and buying land there sets the stage for the tragedy involving Dinah in the next chapter. His choice to linger in Canaan's cities rather than press on has consequences.

interpretationNotes.claim: The reconciliation of the estranged brothers, sealed with weeping and an unreturned gift, is read in the Catholic tradition as a portrait of grace healing broken relationships, where seeing a forgiving face becomes "as though I had seen the face of God" and points toward the reconciliation God offers humanity.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers embrace the same theme of grace transforming enemies into brothers and often draw the identical link to the prodigal's homecoming. Both traditions read Esau's mercy as evidence of God answering Jacob's prayer, and neither treats Jacob's diplomatic care as diminishing the genuineness of the reconciliation.
